## Introduction

Emotion is an embodied experience, involving interaction between mind and body (Barrett & Lindquist, 2008; Damasio & Carvalho, 2013). Contemporary models of emotion diverge in whether the bodily changes associated with emotions follow a universal pattern (Barrett et al., 2006; Kreibig, 2010; Volynets et al., 2020). A series of research explored universality of how people associate different emotions with bodily sensations across 15 countries (Nummenmaa et al., 2014; Volynets et al., 2020). In particular, for the replication project, I focus on the experiment 1c from Nummenmaa et al. (2014), where they conducted a comparison between two different cultural groups: Finnish-Taiwanese (N=36). These groups differ more substantially in both cultural and linguistic distance than the two groups in experiment 1b (Finnish-Swedish,) and the small sample size makes the replication feasible within the short time frame. However, recruiting Finnish and Taiwanese participants is challenging, and our research team lacks sufficient language proficiency to interpret responses from these groups with confidence. To address this, I propose to conceptually replicate the study using two culturally distant populations that are more accessible: native English-speaking Americans and Koreans. 

Nummenmaa et al. (2014) included two independent variables - the type of emotion words (basic vs nonbasic; measured within-subject), and the culture group (Finnish vs Taiwanese; measured between-subject). For replicating experiment 1c, we focused on the second variable, the culture group differences, specifically, whether the Spearman correlation between embodied emotion representation of two participants from different cultures are larger within the basic emotion categories (matched condition; anger-Finnish vs anger-Taiwanese) than that of between-category (mismatched condition; anger-Finnish vs happiness-Taiwanese).The effect size between the two conditions and the variability measures are not reported in the study, and the data of the original paper was not accessible to the original paper's authors. Therefore, the replication objective was to replicating the correlation values of the two conditions.

In addition, we conducted exploratory analyses extending beyond the original study. Specifically, we applied the same procedures to within-cultural participant pairs (i.e., two native Korean-speaking participants or two native English-speaking participants). Using the correlation values from matched and mismatched emotion conditions in these within-cultural pairs, we also explored differences between within-culture and between-culture similarity patterns.

One anticipated challenge in running this experiment on Prolific is accurately identifying participants’ cultural backgrounds. Especially for Korean speakers recruited through prolific, it is highly likely that they are equally proficient in English or more familiar with the Western cultural context. To mitigate this, a language background survey will be attached, in addition to the body representation task, so that we can accurately identify the target culture group.

It is expected for Korean participants recruited from prolific to also have some English exposure or regular usage of English in their everyday lives. ## Methods

### Reliability and Validity
The experiment that I plan to replicate (experiment 1c) did not report any reliability or validity related measures. However, experiment 1b and experiment 1c were attemps to measure whether the trend observed in experiment 1 generalizes to other cultures, especially for the basic emotions. Therefore, the experiment 1c itself is an attempt to check the external validity.


### Power Analysis

Power analysis was not feasible because the original paper did not report the effect size, nor the original data was accessible. Therefore, this replication closely followed the sample size of the original experiment.

### Planned Sample

Following the sample size in Nummenmaa et al. (2014), 36 participants were collected, with 18 participants in each cultural group (United States, Korea.) To recruit two separate culture group, two separate prolific studies were created. To filter Korean participants, First Language-Korean, Primary Language-Korean, and Nationality-Korean filters were applied in prolific. To filter native English speakers from USA, Primary Language-English, First Language-English, and Nationality-United States filters were applied in prolific. Although there are only a small number of eligible Korean participants, recruiting 18 participants is practically feasible.

Since the estimated completion time is around 10 minutes, the compensation will be 1/6 of the average between the minimum California hourly wage and the federal hourly rage (\$12/hour in average): each participant were be paid \$2.00.

### Materials

To measure the embodied representation of emotion, "Bodily Sensation Maps (BSM)" will be used, where participants will color body regions where they feel increased or decreased bodily activity for each emotion word presented. Six basic (anger, fear, disgust, happiness, sadness, and surprise) emotions, as well as a neutral state, will be presented. Web-based version of the BSM measure was created using the code provided in their repository ([link](https://version.aalto.fi/gitlab/eglerean/embody/-/tree/master/v1?ref_type=heads)), along with some minor changes wordings of the instructions. Unlike the original version, I also modified the code so that drawing outside of the body silhouette was not allowed or stored as data. Two versions of the experiment (one for the Korean speaking participants, and one for English speaking participants) were created, as experiment 1c also translated their materials into the respective languages that each cultural group speaks. Everything else remains the same with the original experiment, including the brush size, and the exact red and blue colors for indicating activation and deactivation, and the randomization of word orders.

In addition to the BSM measure, language background survey was attached at the end to accurately identify the target culture group. For assessing the language background, subscales from the Language Experience and Proficiency Questionnaire (LEAP-Q, Marian et al., 2007) will be used. The scales include the number of languages the participants speak, the order of acquisition and dominance of each languages they can speak, self-rated proficiency, and the context of usage of the listed languages.

### Procedure	

Participants were presented with two silhouettes of bodies alongside one of the seven emotion words (six basic emotions or neutral), and was asked to color the bodily regions were they felt activated or deactivated when feeling the given emotion. Then, they will fill out the language background survey.

### Analysis Plan

The resulting data from Bodily Sensation Maps (BSM) measure were stored in a separate server, with each response as a group of coordinates indicating the participants' brush touch. Using the preprocessing code provided by the authors, these groups of coordinates were converted to matrices storing count information in each pixel. Data from both bodies (the left body indicating activation, the right body indicating deactivation) consisted of 50,364 pixels each, with pixels only inside the body were calculated.

Exclusion criteria were attention check failures, trial completion time, and the drawing pattern shown in the BSM data. First, if the data points from participants failing any of the two attention checks were excluded. Moreover, data points from participants who had more than one trial completed in less than 5 seconds were excluded. Lastly, by visualizing each participant's responses for each emotion, drawings exhibiting the similar response across 70% or more of the conditions (5 emotions out of 7) in both bodies, or exhibiting significant overlap in deactivation and activation responses in more than one condition, were excluded from the final analyses.

Following Nummenmaa et al. (2014), the similarity between the two emotion-wise BSMs from two participants were measured through pixel-wise correlation (Spearman's rank correlation). Zero values in the heatmaps (i.e., regions without paint) were filled with Gaussian noise to avoid inflated correlations. Pixels outside the body silhouette were masked and not considered for analysis. For every possible cross-cultural participant pair (i.e., one native Korean and one native English-speaking participant), correlations for both matched-emotion BSMs (e.g., sadness–sadness) and mismatched-emotion BSMs (e.g., sadness–anger) were computed. Although we initially planned to compare the resulting correlation distributions using a t-test to evaluate differences between matched and mismatched conditions, we ultimately did not conduct this test because the correlations in both conditions were negligibly small. Although some details of the analysis pipeline were not fully specified in the original paper, the procedure described here is inferred from the results of Experiment 1c.

### Differences from Original Study

In this conceptual replication, we recruited Korean participants and native English speakers from USA, due to the challenge in recruiting Finnish and Taiwanese participants through prolific, and our research team lacking sufficient language proficiency to interpret responses from these groups with confidence. It is highly likely that the Korean participants recruited through prolific are as equally proficient in English or more familiar to Western cultural context. It could be expected that the differences between within and between culture correlation will be smaller in the replication sample than that of the data from Nummenmaa et al. (2014).

Moreover, stricter exclusion criteria were contrived, given that this replication was conducted online. It is unclear whether the original experiment was conducted in-person or online, but since the original study used manual inspection to remove anomalous painting behavior, this project applies stricter criteria beyond the manual inspection for clearer criteria.

### Methods Addendum (Post Data Collection)

#### Actual Sample
  Among 36 datapoints, 7 were excluded for the final analysis, according to the data exclusions spelled out in analysis plan. As a result, this project ended up undersampling than the original study, but the main trend were very similar when we used the full sample without exclusion, which will be discussed below.

Below is the exclusion result based on the drawing data (BSM).
  
```{python}  
# get the list of participants from the drawing data
import os

base_path = r"../data/final_data/drawing_data_raw/"

csv_counts = {}
duration= {}

# Loop through all items in the base directory
for item in os.listdir(base_path):
    dir_path = os.path.join(base_path, item)

    # Only process directories
    if os.path.isdir(dir_path):
        # Count CSV files inside this directory
        count = sum(1 for f in os.listdir(dir_path) if f.lower().endswith(".csv"))
        csv_counts[item] = count

        # Only process duration if participant has 7 trials (8 files including timestamp.csv)
        if count == 8:
            timestamp_path = os.path.join(dir_path, "timestamps.csv")

            if os.path.exists(timestamp_path):
                df = pd.read_csv(timestamp_path)

                # compute duration per trial (in milliseconds)
                df["duration_ms"] = df["submit_timestamp"] - df["start_timestamp"]

                # store as dictionary: {trial_id: duration}
                duration[item] = dict(zip(df["trial_id"], df["duration_ms"]))

# Print summary
print("CSV counts:", csv_counts)
print("Durations:", duration)
```

```{python}  
import os
import pandas as pd

overlap_base = r"../data/final_data/both_sides_counts/"

overlaps = {}   # {participant_id_from_filename: {condition: overlap_value}}

for fname in os.listdir(overlap_base):
    if not fname.lower().endswith(".txt"):
        continue

    # participant ID from filename (e.g., "5c1980c24a03080001139d5a_bothSides.txt")
    pid = fname.split('_')[0]
    fpath = os.path.join(overlap_base, fname)

    # Let pandas auto-detect the delimiter
    df = pd.read_csv(fpath, sep=None, engine="python")

    # Use the last (or only) row
    row = df.iloc[-1]

    # Drop the first column value (the embedded ID under 'Neutral')
    # Keep overlaps for actual emotion conditions
    values = row[1:]  # everything except the first column

    # Force numeric conversion (just in case)
    values = pd.to_numeric(values, errors='coerce')

    # Store as dict: {condition_name: overlap_value}
    cond_names = df.columns[1:]  # skip the first column name
    cond_dict = dict(zip(cond_names, values))

    overlaps[pid] = cond_dict

print("Loaded overlap counts for", len(overlaps), "participants")

# Optional sanity check on one participant:
example_pid = next(iter(overlaps)) if overlaps else None
if example_pid:
    print("Example participant:", example_pid)
    print(overlaps[example_pid])

```


```{python}  
# Participants who show "lots of positive/negative overlap in more than one emotion condition

exclude_overlap = []

OVERLAP_THRESHOLD = 1000 

for pid, cond_dict in overlaps.items():
    # Count how many conditions exceed the threshold (ignoring NaN)
    n_big_overlaps = sum(
        (v > OVERLAP_THRESHOLD) 
        for v in cond_dict.values() 
        if pd.notna(v)
    )
    if n_big_overlaps > 1:
        exclude_overlap.append(pid)

print("Participants excluded for overlap:", exclude_overlap)
print("Number excluded for overlap:", len(exclude_overlap))

survey = survey[~survey["userID"].isin(exclude_overlap)]

n_after_overlap_filter = len(survey)

print(n_after_overlap_filter)
```

### Data storage
  Raw data is stored in a local server and a qualtrics server. For the pilot data, the last two characters of the prolific IDs were altered. For the data from the main experiment, all participants were renamed as re-assigning anonymized IDs. Only the anonymized data was shared on github.

#### Differences from pre-data collection methods plan
  None

## Results

### Pilot experiments
Two pilot study was conducted to confirm the paradigm is working as desired, and to make sure the data is being saved correctly. For pilot A, two datapoints were collected amonst the students taking "PSYC201A" class at UCSD. the processing of the drawing data seemed successful, as shown by the visualization of one of the participants' responses. The detailed explanation of preprocessing method is described in the next section.

Moreover, exclusions were performed to test the appropriateness of the exclusion criteria. The resulting exclusions are presented below.

```{python}
# ---
# Drawing data is pre-processed using a matlab script, provided by the original paper's authors.
# Data Preparation: additional processing of the pre-processed drawing data (.mat files)
# ---

import os
import math
import numpy as np
import scipy.io
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from matplotlib.colors import ListedColormap
import matplotlib.cm as cm
import matplotlib.gridspec as gridspec
import matplotlib.image as mpimg
from skimage.transform import resize

# -----------------------------------------------------
# Load emotion labels
# -----------------------------------------------------
labels = [
    'Neutral', 'Fear', 'Anger', 'Disgust', 'Sadness', 'Happiness', 'Surprise'
]

raw_maps = {}  # structure: {subject_id: {emotion_label: 2D numpy array}}

# -----------------------------------------------------
# Choose which preprocessed files to load
# -----------------------------------------------------
basepath = r'../data/pilotA/preprocessed_data/'

files = sorted([f for f in os.listdir(basepath) if f.endswith('.mat')])

NS = len(files)
NC = 7

# -----------------------------------------------------
# Load MATLAB data into python dictionary
# -----------------------------------------------------
for s, fname in enumerate(files):
    subject_id = fname.split('_')[0]
    mat = scipy.io.loadmat(os.path.join(basepath, fname))
    resmat = mat['resmat']  # shape: [H, W, NC]

    raw_maps[subject_id] = {}

    for n in range(NC):
        subj_map = resmat[:, :, n]
        raw = np.copy(subj_map)

        emotion_label = labels[n].replace(" ", "_").lower()
        raw_maps[subject_id][emotion_label] = raw


# -----------------------------------------------------
# Load base silhouette and mask
# -----------------------------------------------------
base = mpimg.imread('../data/files_for_preprocessing/base.png')
mask = mpimg.imread('../data/files_for_preprocessing/mask.png')  # α mask: 0–255 or 0–1

# MATLAB→Python corrected crop (inclusive in MATLAB → end-exclusive in Python)
base2 = base[10:532, 33:204, :]

# Normalize mask range
mask_f = mask.astype(float)
if mask_f.max() > 1:
    mask_f = mask_f / 255.0
# If mask is RGB, convert to single channel
if mask_f.ndim == 3:
    mask_f = mask_f[:, :, 0]

# -----------------------------------------------------
# Pick a subject to plot
# -----------------------------------------------------
subject_id = list(raw_maps.keys())[0]
print(f"Plotting subject: {subject_id}")

emotion_keys = list(raw_maps[subject_id].keys())
H_map, W_map = raw_maps[subject_id][emotion_keys[0]].shape
H_base, W_base = base2.shape[:2]

if (H_map, W_map) != (H_base, W_base):
    raise ValueError(
        f"ERROR: Map size {H_map}x{W_map} does not match silhouette size {H_base}x{W_base}.\n"
        "Remove resizing only if they already match."
    )

# -----------------------------------------------------
# Build custom diverging colormap
# -----------------------------------------------------
NumCol = 64
hot = cm.hot(np.linspace(0, 1, NumCol))[:, :3]
cold = np.flipud(hot[:, ::-1])
neutral = np.zeros((2 * round(NumCol * 0.05), 3))
lut = np.vstack([cold, neutral, hot])
final_cmap = ListedColormap(lut)

# compute symmetric intensity bound
all_vals = np.hstack([raw_maps[subject_id][emo].ravel() for emo in emotion_keys])
M = np.max(np.abs(all_vals))
print("Symmetric intensity scale limit M =", M)

# -----------------------------------------------------
# Plot body maps (mask-aware RGBA overlay + safe title spacing)
# -----------------------------------------------------
ncols = 7
nrows = math.ceil(NC / ncols)

fig = plt.figure(figsize=(2.5 * ncols + 2, 2.5 * nrows))
gs = gridspec.GridSpec(
    nrows, ncols + 1,
    width_ratios=[1] * ncols + [0.18],
    wspace=0.05, hspace=0.25
)

for idx, emo in enumerate(emotion_keys):
    row = idx // ncols
    col = idx % ncols
    ax = fig.add_subplot(gs[row, col])

    # Draw silhouette
    ax.imshow(base2, zorder=0)

    # ===== Mask-aware RGBA overlay (no black square) =====
    data = raw_maps[subject_id][emo]  # H×W
    # normalize to [0,1] consistent with vmin=-M, vmax=M
    normed = np.clip((data + M) / (2 * M), 0, 1)
    rgba = final_cmap(normed)          # H×W×4
    rgba[..., 3] = mask_f               # alpha = body mask (0 outside, 1 inside)
    ax.imshow(rgba, interpolation='nearest', zorder=1)

    ax.set_title(emo, fontsize=9)
    ax.axis('off')

# Blank unused subplots
for idx in range(NC, nrows * ncols):
    fig.add_subplot(gs[idx // ncols, idx % ncols]).axis('off')

# Colorbar
cax = fig.add_subplot(gs[:, -1])
sm = plt.cm.ScalarMappable(cmap=final_cmap, norm=plt.Normalize(vmin=-M, vmax=M))
sm.set_array([])
plt.colorbar(sm, cax=cax)
cax.set_ylabel("Intensity", rotation=270, labelpad=12)

# Title & layout — avoid overlap, avoid tight_layout warning
fig.suptitle(f"Emotion Body Maps (Subject {subject_id})", fontsize=18)

# Move the figure content downward so the title sits above it
fig.subplots_adjust(top=0.8)

plt.show()

```

For pilot B, a sample of 3 participants is collected from prolific. After pilot A, the exclusion criteria of trial duration were added. The resulting exclusions based on completion, two attention checks, and trial duration are presented below.

```{python}
print(f"Plotting subject: {subject_id}")

emotion_keys = list(raw_maps[subject_id].keys())
H_map, W_map = raw_maps[subject_id][emotion_keys[0]].shape
H_base, W_base = base2.shape[:2]

if (H_map, W_map) != (H_base, W_base):
    raise ValueError(
        f"ERROR: Map size {H_map}x{W_map} does not match silhouette size {H_base}x{W_base}.\n"
        "Remove resizing only if they already match."
    )

# -----------------------------------------------------
# Build custom diverging colormap
# -----------------------------------------------------
NumCol = 64
hot = cm.hot(np.linspace(0, 1, NumCol))[:, :3]
cold = np.flipud(hot[:, ::-1])
neutral = np.zeros((2 * round(NumCol * 0.05), 3))
lut = np.vstack([cold, neutral, hot])
final_cmap = ListedColormap(lut)

# compute symmetric intensity bound
all_vals = np.hstack([raw_maps[subject_id][emo].ravel() for emo in emotion_keys])
M = np.max(np.abs(all_vals))
print("Symmetric intensity scale limit M =", M)

# -----------------------------------------------------
# Plot body maps (mask-aware RGBA overlay + safe title spacing)
# -----------------------------------------------------
ncols = 7
nrows = math.ceil(NC / ncols)

fig = plt.figure(figsize=(2.5 * ncols + 2, 2.5 * nrows))
gs = gridspec.GridSpec(
    nrows, ncols + 1,
    width_ratios=[1] * ncols + [0.18],
    wspace=0.05, hspace=0.25
)

for idx, emo in enumerate(emotion_keys):
    row = idx // ncols
    col = idx % ncols
    ax = fig.add_subplot(gs[row, col])

    # Draw silhouette
    ax.imshow(base2, zorder=0)

    # ===== Mask-aware RGBA overlay (no black square) =====
    data = raw_maps[subject_id][emo]  # H×W
    # normalize to [0,1] consistent with vmin=-M, vmax=M
    normed = np.clip((data + M) / (2 * M), 0, 1)
    rgba = final_cmap(normed)          # H×W×4
    rgba[..., 3] = mask_f               # alpha = body mask (0 outside, 1 inside)
    ax.imshow(rgba, interpolation='nearest', zorder=1)

    ax.set_title(emo, fontsize=9)
    ax.axis('off')

# Blank unused subplots
for idx in range(NC, nrows * ncols):
    fig.add_subplot(gs[idx // ncols, idx % ncols]).axis('off')

# Colorbar
cax = fig.add_subplot(gs[:, -1])
sm = plt.cm.ScalarMappable(cmap=final_cmap, norm=plt.Normalize(vmin=-M, vmax=M))
sm.set_array([])
plt.colorbar(sm, cax=cax)
cax.set_ylabel("Intensity", rotation=270, labelpad=12)

# Title & layout — avoid overlap, avoid tight_layout warning
fig.suptitle(f"Emotion Body Maps (Subject {subject_id})", fontsize=18)

# Move the figure content downward so the title sits above it
fig.subplots_adjust(top=0.8)

plt.show()
```

Both pilot experiments were performed on English speakers from U.S., using the paradigm for English speakers. The paradigm for Korean speakers remained the same except for the emotion words, which were translated to Korean. 

### Data preparation

Data preparation will follow the procedure described in the 'Analysis plan' section. Matlab code provided by the authors of the papers (in this [link](https://version.aalto.fi/gitlab/eglerean/embody/-/tree/master/matlab?ref_type=heads])) will be imported to follow the exact procedure used from the paper. The code provided involves preprocessing the raw BSM data, which is loading the count vectors, performing Gaussian smoothing to simulate the brush size, and Subtract ‘deactivation’ values from ‘activation’ values to create a combined BSM map for each emotion per participant. THe matlab code used for preprocessing is pasted below:


```{matlab}
%% Modified from: "Short matlab demo to load and visualize emBODY data"
%
% - Please note that there are hard-coded parameters related to our
% experiment version. If you modify the graphic layout of the web tool you
% will need to change also how matlab preprocesses the data
% - In our experiment we treated the left part of the screen as positive
% values and the right part as negative values, and performed a subtraction
% between the two. You are free to use the whole painting area and you
% don't need to subtract the values if left and right silouhettes have
% different meanings than activation/deactivation.
% - The demo uses the function load_subj, make sure it is in your path
% - It should be easy to rewrite this in python for those without a Matlab
% license.
%
% Code by Enrico Glerean and Lauri Nummenmaa
%
% Thanks to Laura Harrison @ caltech for useful feedback

% let's begin
close all
clear all

% get a list of subjects
cd('C:/Users/lovel/Documents/Embodiment/data_analysis/embody_matlab');
basepath='../embody_matlab/drawing_data_prolific'; % folder where the subject data is a
subjects=dir([basepath '\*']);
subjects = subjects(~ismember({subjects.name},{'.','..'})); % remove . and ..
disp("Folder names:");
disp({subjects.name}');

%%% code added - to deal with incomplete drawing data
% --- Filter subjects based on vocab_test_result.csv ---
% vocab_file = fullfile('../data_analysis/vocab_test_result.csv');
vocab_file = fullfile('../data_analysis/prolific_id_list.csv');
if isfile(vocab_file)
    % If file exists, filter subjects based on CSV
    subjtbl = readtable(vocab_file);      % read CSV into table
    valid_ids = string(subjtbl.id);       % list of allowed subject IDs (from "id" column)
    disp("Valid IDs from csv:");
    disp(valid_ids);

    % keep only subfolders that match IDs
    isub = [subjects(:).isdir]; 
    subjects = subjects(isub);                           % only folders
    subjects = subjects(~ismember({subjects.name},{'.','..'})); % remove . and ..
    folder_names = strtrim(string({subjects.name}));     % normalize folder names
    subjects = subjects(ismember(folder_names, valid_ids));  % keep only valid IDs

    disp("Remaining valid subject folders:");
    disp({subjects.name}');

else
    % If file is missing, proceed without filtering
    warning('vocab_test_result.csv not found. Proceeding without subject filtering.');

    % keep all valid subfolders
    isub = [subjects(:).isdir]; 
    subjects = subjects(isub);
    subjects = subjects(~ismember({subjects.name},{'.','..'})); % remove . and ..
    disp("Proceeding with all subject folders:");
    disp({subjects.name}');
end
% -------------------------------------------------------

% the base image used for painting (in our case only one sided since we
% subtract values)
base=uint8(imread('base.png'));
base2=base(10:531,33:203,:); % single image base
labels={'Neutral'
'Fear'
'Anger'
'Disgust'
'Sadness'
'Happiness'
'Surprise'
'Anxiety'
'Love'
'Depression'
'Contempt'
'Pride'
'Shame'
'Jealousy'
};
mask=imread('mask.png');

% for each subject, load data
for s=1:length(subjects)
    % skip dot and dotdot folders
    if(strcmp(subjects(s).name(1),'.')) continue; end 

    %% Data loading
    % let's load the subject's answers into a variable a
    data=load_subj([basepath '\' subjects(s).name]);
    NC=length(data); % number of conditions
    
    %% Painting reconstruction
    % 'data' now contains all mouse movements. What we need are the mouse
    % locations while the button was pressed (i.e. during painting)
    % Furthermore, the painting tool has a brush size. We recreate that
    % using image filter
    
    for n=1:NC;
        T=length(data(n).paint(:,2)); % number of mouse locations
        over=zeros(size(base,1),size(base,2)); % empty matrix to reconstruct painting
        for t=1:T
            y=ceil(data(n).paint(t,3)+1);
            x=ceil(data(n).paint(t,2)+1);
            if(x<=0) x=1; end
            if(y<=0) y=1; end
            if(x>=900) x=900; end % hardcoded for our experiment, you need to change it if you changed layout
            if(y>=600) y=600; end % hardcoded for our experiment, you need to change it if you changed layout
            over(y,x)=over(y,x)+1;
        end
        % Simulate brush size with a gaussian disk
        h=fspecial('gaussian',[15 15],5);
        over=imfilter(over,h);

        %%% modified: the number of pixels that both the left and right %%%%
        %%% part are painted (both positive and negative) %%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%

        % Extract left and right areas
        left  = over(10:531,33:203);
        right = over(10:531,696:866);
        
        % Threshold for "painted"
        th = 0;   % consider anything > 0 as painted; change if needed
        
        leftMask  = left  > th;
        rightMask = right > th;
        
        % Pixels painted on BOTH left and right sides
        bothMask  = leftMask & rightMask;
        numBoth   = nnz(bothMask);   % the number you want to export
        
        % Store per condition
        numBothPerCond(n) = numBoth;
        
        % Continue with your original subtraction
        over2 = left - right;
        resmat(:,:,n) = over2;

        %%% modification ends %%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%

        % we subtract left part minus right part of painted area
        % values are hard-coded to our web layout
        over2=over(10:531,33:203,:)-over(10:531,696:866,:);
        resmat(:,:,n)=over2;
    end
    
    %% store result    
    %outdir = fullfile('..\embody_matlab\preprocessed_data_addition_1104');
    outdir = fullfile('..\embody_matlab\preprocessed_data_prolific');
    if ~exist(outdir,'dir')
        mkdir(outdir);
    end

    if exist('resmat','var') && ~isempty(resmat)
        save(fullfile(outdir, [subjects(s).name '_preprocessed.mat']), 'resmat');
    else
        warning('resmat is empty for subject %s', subjects(s).name);
    end

    %{
    %% visualize subject's data
    M=max(abs(resmat(:))); % max range for colorbar
    NumCol=64;
    hotmap=hot(NumCol);
    coldmap=flipud([hotmap(:,3) hotmap(:,2) hotmap(:,1) ]);
    hotcoldmap=[
        coldmap
        hotmap
    ];

    % note that - for statistical maps - if you want to hide non
    % significant values and show them as black, you need to tweak the
    % colormap so that you have more rows of black between around the
    % non-significant interval. 
    % As an example if we had a threshold, uncomment the below
    if(0)
        th=0.2*M; % just an example threshold, since this is not a statistical map 
        non_sig=round(th/M*NumCol); % proportion of non significant colors
        hotmap=hot(NumCol-non_sig);
        coldmap=flipud([hotmap(:,3) hotmap(:,2) hotmap(:,1) ]);
        hotcoldmap=[
            coldmap
            zeros(2*non_sig,3);
            hotmap
        ];
    end

    %%% modified: save the negative and positive overlap %%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%
    % Save numBothPerCond as a row in a .txt file
    txtOutDir = fullfile(outdir, 'both_sides_counts');
    if ~exist(txtOutDir, 'dir')
        mkdir(txtOutDir);
    end
    
    % Create header (condition names)
    header = strjoin(labels', '\t');
    
    % Prepare row: participant name + numbers
    rowData = [subjects(s).name, sprintf('\t%d', numBothPerCond)];
    
    % Write to file
    fid = fopen(fullfile(txtOutDir, [subjects(s).name '_bothSides.txt']), 'w');
    fprintf(fid, '%s\n', header);
    fprintf(fid, '%s\n', rowData);
    fclose(fid);

    %%% modification ends %%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%
end

```

The resulting preprocessed data (.mat format) was imported into Python environment, processed and visualized individually for the sanity check. 

First, It was processed into a dictionary of coordinate values by each pixel.

```{python}
import scipy
import os
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

labels = [
    'Neutral', 'Fear', 'Anger', 'Disgust', 'Sadness', 'Happiness', 'Surprise'
]

raw_maps = {}  # final structure: {subject_id: {emotion_label: 2D numpy array}}

basepath = '../data/final_data/drawing_data_preprocessed'

files = sorted([f for f in os.listdir(basepath) if f.endswith('.mat')])
NS = len(files)
NC = len(labels)

for s, fname in enumerate(files):
    subject_id = fname.split('_')[0]

    mat = scipy.io.loadmat(os.path.join(basepath, fname))  
    resmat = mat['resmat']  # shape: [H, W, NC]

    raw_maps[subject_id] = {}

    for n in range(NC):
        subj_map = resmat[:, :, n]

        raw = np.copy(subj_map)

        emotion_label = labels[n].replace(" ", "_").lower()
        raw_maps[subject_id][emotion_label] = raw
```

Then, the data was masked to ensure that pixels outside the body silhouette not to be considered for analysis (it was converted to nan values, as compared to 0 which could mean it's a valid pixel but was unpainted by the participant.)

```{python}
import matplotlib.image as mpimg
#load the mask

mask_img = mpimg.imread('../data/files_for_preprocessing/mask.png')

if mask_img.ndim == 3:
    mask_img = mask_img[..., 0]
mask = (mask_img > 0.5).astype(np.uint8)  # uint8 for resize
H, W = mask.shape
print(f"Original mask size: {H}×{W}, valid pixels: {mask.sum()}")

#resize the mask
# Get size from one of the raw maps
any_subj = next(iter(raw_maps))
any_emo = next(iter(raw_maps[any_subj]))
H_raw, W_raw = raw_maps[any_subj][any_emo].shape

H_mask, W_mask= H, W

# Resize mask if dimensions do NOT match
if (H_mask, W_mask) != (H_raw, W_raw):
    mask_resized = cv2.resize(
        mask.astype(float),
        (W_raw, H_raw),
        interpolation=cv2.INTER_NEAREST
    )
    mask_resized = (mask_resized > 0.5).astype(np.uint8)
else:
    mask_resized = mask
# filter out datapoints outside the body using the mask
masked_maps = {}    # {subject: {emotion: 2D masked array}}

for subj in raw_maps:
    masked_maps[subj] = {}
    for emo in raw_maps[subj]:
        img = raw_maps[subj][emo]
        masked = np.where(mask_resized == 1, img, np.nan)
        masked_maps[subj][emo] = masked
```

Lastly, each participant's BSMs were visualized and stored as separate file for manual inspection.

```{python}
#| eval: false
import os
import math
import numpy as np
import scipy.io
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from matplotlib.colors import ListedColormap
import matplotlib.cm as cm
import matplotlib.gridspec as gridspec
import matplotlib.image as mpimg
from skimage.transform import resize


# -----------------------------------------------------
# Load base silhouette & mask
# -----------------------------------------------------
base = mpimg.imread('../data/files_for_preprocessing/base.png')
mask = mpimg.imread('../data/files_for_preprocessing/mask.png')

# Correct MATLAB → Python crop
base2 = base[10:532, 33:204, :]     # (H_base, W_base, 3)

# Normalize mask
mask_f = mask.astype(float)
if mask_f.max() > 1:
    mask_f /= 255.0
if mask_f.ndim == 3:
    mask_f = mask_f[:, :, 0]
# -----------------------------------------------------
# Pre-compute target map size from first subject
# -----------------------------------------------------
first_subj = list(raw_maps.keys())[0]
H_map, W_map = raw_maps[first_subj][labels[0].lower()].shape
H_base, W_base = base2.shape[:2]

if (H_map, W_map) != (H_base, W_base):
    raise ValueError(
        f"Raw map size {H_map}×{W_map} does not match silhouette {H_base}×{W_base}."
    )

# -----------------------------------------------------
# Build custom diverging LUT
# -----------------------------------------------------
NumCol = 64
hot = cm.hot(np.linspace(0, 1, NumCol))[:, :3]
cold = np.flipud(hot[:, ::-1])
neutral = np.zeros((2 * round(NumCol * 0.05), 3))
lut = np.vstack([cold, neutral, hot])
final_cmap = ListedColormap(lut)


# -----------------------------------------------------
# === LOOP OVER ALL PARTICIPANTS ===
# -----------------------------------------------------
output_dir = "participant_visualizations"
os.makedirs(output_dir, exist_ok=True)

for subject_id in raw_maps.keys():
    print(f"Rendering subject {subject_id} ...")

    emotion_keys = list(raw_maps[subject_id].keys())

    # Compute symmetric color bound for THIS subject
    all_vals = np.hstack([raw_maps[subject_id][emo].ravel() for emo in emotion_keys])
    M = np.max(np.abs(all_vals))

    # Prepare grid
    ncols = 7
    nrows = math.ceil(NC / ncols)

    fig = plt.figure(figsize=(2.5 * ncols + 2, 2.5 * nrows))
    gs = gridspec.GridSpec(
        nrows, ncols + 1,
        width_ratios=[1] * ncols + [0.18],
        wspace=0.05, hspace=0.25
    )

    # --------------------------------------------------
    # Plot each emotion
    # --------------------------------------------------
    for idx, emo in enumerate(emotion_keys):
        row = idx // ncols
        col = idx % ncols
        ax = fig.add_subplot(gs[row, col])

        ax.imshow(base2, zorder=0)

        data = raw_maps[subject_id][emo]
        normed = np.clip((data + M) / (2 * M), 0, 1)

        rgba = final_cmap(normed)
        rgba[..., 3] = mask_f      # mask-aware alpha

        ax.imshow(rgba, interpolation='nearest', zorder=1)
        ax.set_title(emo, fontsize=9)
        ax.axis('off')

    # Empty cells
    for idx in range(NC, nrows * ncols):
        fig.add_subplot(gs[idx // ncols, idx % ncols]).axis('off')

    # Colorbar
    cax = fig.add_subplot(gs[:, -1])
    sm = plt.cm.ScalarMappable(
        cmap=final_cmap,
        norm=plt.Normalize(vmin=-M, vmax=M)
    )
    sm.set_array([])
    plt.colorbar(sm, cax=cax)
    cax.set_ylabel("Intensity", rotation=270, labelpad=12)

    # Title
    fig.suptitle(f"Emotion Body Maps (Subject {subject_id})", fontsize=18)
    fig.subplots_adjust(top=0.8)

    # Save figure
    out_path = os.path.join(output_dir, f"{subject_id}_bsm.png")
    plt.savefig(out_path, dpi=200, bbox_inches='tight')
    plt.close(fig)

print("Done! All participant maps rendered.")
```

```{python}
import pandas as pd
import math

# Load metadata
df = pd.read_csv(
    "../data/final_data/survey/Bodymap_consent_language_history_prolific_id_corrected.csv"
)

# Convert language codes → labels
lang_map = {1: "Korean", 2: "English"}
df["language_label"] = df["language_Kor"].map(lang_map)

# Build lookup: userjID → language_label, skipping NaN IDs
culture_lookup = {}
for sid, lang in zip(df["userID"], df["language_label"]):
    # skip missing / empty IDs
    if pd.isna(sid):
        continue
    sid_str = str(sid)
    culture_lookup[sid_str] = lang

# Get participant IDs directly from masked_maps
mat_ids = list(masked_maps.keys())   # e.g., ["P0", "P1", "ABC25", ...]

mat_ids_set = set(mat_ids)
csv_ids_set = set(culture_lookup.keys())

# Validation (non-fatal)
extra_in_mat = mat_ids_set - csv_ids_set       # present in masked_maps but not CSV

if extra_in_mat:
    print("⚠️ WARNING: IDs in masked_maps NOT found in CSV:", extra_in_mat)

# Build culture list in the *same order* as masked_maps keys
culture_list = []
for sid in mat_ids:
    if sid not in culture_lookup:
        print(f"⚠️ WARNING: ID {sid} not in CSV or was NaN → assigning None")
        culture_list.append(None)
    else:
        culture_list.append(culture_lookup[sid])

# Show aligned output
print("\nAligned culture list:")
for sid, c in zip(mat_ids, culture_list):
    print(f"{sid}  →  {c}")

```

The average body maps across all participants, as well as for each cultural group, were visualized. The general trend seems like much less pixels were colored than the original paper. When averaged emotion maps from each cultures were compared, there seem to have some differences in which body parts are colored more or less across the cultures for some emotion categories (e.g. disgust, sadness, and surprise.)

```{python}
import numpy as np

# Emotion keys in masked_maps (same logic as before)
emotion_keys = [lab.replace(" ", "_").lower() for lab in labels]  # e.g. 'Neutral'→'neutral'

# All subjects in masked_maps (already excluded via your exclusion list)
subject_ids = sorted(masked_maps.keys())

# Split by language
korean_ids = [sid for sid in subject_ids if culture_lookup.get(sid) == "Korean"]
english_ids = [sid for sid in subject_ids if culture_lookup.get(sid) == "English"]

print("Total subjects:", len(subject_ids))
print("Korean subjects:", len(korean_ids))
print("English subjects:", len(english_ids))

# Get spatial size from any subject × emotion
first_subj = subject_ids[0]
H, W = masked_maps[first_subj][emotion_keys[0]].shape
NC = len(emotion_keys)

def compute_group_average(subj_list):
    """
    subj_list: list of subject IDs in this group.
    Returns:
        avg_maps: {emotion_key: 2D array (H, W)} where each value is
                  the NaN-aware mean across participants.
    """
    if len(subj_list) == 0:
        return None
    
    avg_maps = {}
    for emo in emotion_keys:
        # Stack maps across participants: shape (NS_group, H, W)
        stack = []
        for sid in subj_list:
            stack.append(masked_maps[sid][emo])
        stack = np.stack(stack, axis=0)  # (NS_group, H, W)
        
        # NaN-aware mean across subjects
        avg = np.nanmean(stack, axis=0)  # (H, W)
        avg_maps[emo] = avg
    
    return avg_maps

avg_all = compute_group_average(subject_ids)
avg_kor = compute_group_average(korean_ids)
avg_eng = compute_group_average(english_ids)

```

```{python}
import os
import math
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import matplotlib.cm as cm
from matplotlib.colors import ListedColormap
import matplotlib.gridspec as gridspec
import matplotlib.image as mpimg
import numpy as np

# -----------------------------------------------------
# Load base silhouette & mask
# -----------------------------------------------------
base = mpimg.imread('../data/files_for_preprocessing/base.png')
mask = mpimg.imread('../data/files_for_preprocessing/mask.png')

# Crop base exactly as you did before
base2 = base[10:532, 33:204, :]     # (H_base, W_base, 3)

# Normalize mask
mask_f = mask.astype(float)
if mask_f.max() > 1:
    mask_f /= 255.0
if mask_f.ndim == 3:
    mask_f = mask_f[:, :, 0]

H_base, W_base = base2.shape[:2]
assert (H, W) == (H_base, W_base), f"Map size {H}×{W} != silhouette {H_base}×{W_base}"

# -----------------------------------------------------
# Build custom diverging LUT (same as your code)
# -----------------------------------------------------
NumCol = 64
hot = cm.hot(np.linspace(0, 1, NumCol))[:, :3]
cold = np.flipud(hot[:, ::-1])
neutral = np.zeros((2 * round(NumCol * 0.05), 3))
lut = np.vstack([cold, neutral, hot])
final_cmap = ListedColormap(lut)

pretty_labels = labels  

# -----------------------------------------------------
# Helper: plot average maps for one group
# -----------------------------------------------------
def plot_group_averages(avg_maps, group_label, output_dir="group_averaged_maps"):
    """
    avg_maps: {emotion_key: 2D array (H, W)} as returned by compute_group_average
    group_label: 'All', 'Korean', 'English', etc.
    """
    if avg_maps is None:
        print(f"No participants in group {group_label}, skipping.")
        return

    os.makedirs(output_dir, exist_ok=True)

    # Collect all values to define a symmetric color range
    all_vals_list = []
    for emo in emotion_keys:
        arr = avg_maps[emo]
        all_vals_list.append(arr.ravel())
    all_vals = np.concatenate(all_vals_list)
    all_vals = all_vals[~np.isnan(all_vals)]

    if all_vals.size == 0:
        print(f"No valid data in group {group_label}.")
        return

    M = np.max(np.abs(all_vals))  # symmetric bound: [-M, M]

    ncols = 7
    nrows = math.ceil(NC / ncols)

    fig = plt.figure(figsize=(2.5 * ncols + 2, 2.5 * nrows))
    gs = gridspec.GridSpec(
        nrows, ncols + 1,
        width_ratios=[1] * ncols + [0.18],
        wspace=0.05, hspace=0.25
    )

    # Plot each emotion
    for idx, emo in enumerate(emotion_keys):
        row = idx // ncols
        col = idx % ncols
        ax = fig.add_subplot(gs[row, col])

        ax.imshow(base2, zorder=0)

        data = avg_maps[emo]  # averaged raw values (H, W)

        # Normalize to [0,1] for LUT
        normed = (data + M) / (2 * M)
        normed = np.clip(normed, 0, 1)

        rgba = final_cmap(normed)
        rgba[..., 3] = mask_f   # alpha from mask

        ax.imshow(rgba, interpolation='nearest', zorder=1)
        ax.set_title(pretty_labels[idx], fontsize=9)
        ax.axis('off')

    # Empty cells if NC < nrows * ncols
    for idx in range(NC, nrows * ncols):
        fig.add_subplot(gs[idx // ncols, idx % ncols]).axis('off')

    # Colorbar
    cax = fig.add_subplot(gs[:, -1])
    sm = plt.cm.ScalarMappable(
        cmap=final_cmap,
        norm=plt.Normalize(vmin=-M, vmax=M)
    )
    sm.set_array([])
    plt.colorbar(sm, cax=cax)
    cax.set_ylabel("Mean intensity (raw units)", rotation=270, labelpad=12)

    # Title
    fig.suptitle(f"Average Emotion Body Maps ({group_label})", fontsize=18)
    fig.subplots_adjust(top=0.8)

    # Save
    out_path = os.path.join(output_dir, f"{group_label}_avg_maps.png")
    plt.savefig(out_path, dpi=200, bbox_inches='tight')
    plt.show()
    print(f"Saved {group_label} average maps to:", out_path)

# -----------------------------------------------------
# Make figures for All / Korean / English
# -----------------------------------------------------
plot_group_averages(avg_all, "All")
plot_group_averages(avg_kor, "Korean")
plot_group_averages(avg_eng, "English")

print("Done! Group-averaged raw maps rendered.")

```

### Confirmatory Analysis
For confirmatory analysis, pixel-wise Spearman correlations will be computed. First, list of of all possible pairs of two participants were collected. Then, for each pair of participants, correlations of the BSMs of all possible pairs of mismatched emotions (for example, sadness and anger) and matched emotions (for example, sadness and sadness) were computed and stored. Here, the correlations are computed only among valid pixels, which means that the 'masked' coordinates were used for analysis. Moreover, for uncolored pixels within the body silhouette, Gaussian noise were filled instead of 0 values to prevent inflating the correlations.

```{python}
# apply Gaussian noise - except for the masked area

processed_maps = {}   # {subject: {emotion: 1D vector}}
noise_std = 1e-6

for subj in masked_maps:
    processed_maps[subj] = {}

    for emo in masked_maps[subj]:
        
        img = masked_maps[subj][emo]   # 2D masked map with NaNs
        img2 = img.copy()

        # Only replace ZERO values that are NOT NaN
        zero_mask = (img2 == 0) & (~np.isnan(img2))

        # Generate noise only where needed
        img2[zero_mask] = np.random.normal(0, noise_std, size=np.sum(zero_mask))

        # Flatten for correlation (NaNs preserved)
        processed_maps[subj][emo] = img2.reshape(-1)
        
#get the list of subject pairs
from itertools import combinations

subject_pairs = list(combinations(subject_ids, 2))  
print("Number of unique subject pairs:", len(subject_pairs))

```

```{python}
import os
import pandas as pd
from scipy.stats import spearmanr
import numpy as np

output_path = "../data/final_data/analysis_results/final_data_correlations_after_exclusion.csv"

# 1. INITIALIZE pair_rows (depending on what's available)

# Case A: pair_rows is already in memory
if "pair_rows" in globals() and isinstance(pair_rows, list):
    print(f"pair_rows already exists in memory with {len(pair_rows)} rows.")
    in_memory = True

# Case B: no pair_rows but CSV exists → load progress
elif os.path.exists(output_path):
    print(f"Loading previous progress from {output_path} ...")
    df_prev = pd.read_csv(output_path)
    pair_rows = df_prev.to_dict("records")
    print(f"Loaded {len(pair_rows)} previously computed rows.")
    in_memory = False

# Case C: no pair_rows and no CSV → start fresh
else:
    print("No existing progress found. Initializing empty pair_rows.")
    pair_rows = []
    in_memory = False


# 2. BUILD SKIP SET FROM EXISTING pair_rows

done_keys = set(
    (row["subj_i"], row["subj_j"], row["emotion1"], row["emotion2"])
    for row in pair_rows
)

print(f"Resuming computation with {len(done_keys)} correlations already completed.")

# 3. MAIN LOOP — masked correlations using existing NaNs

n_pair = 0
n_new = 0
SAVE_INTERVAL = 30
total_pairs = len(subject_pairs)

for subj_i, subj_j in subject_pairs:
    n_pair += 1

    culture_i = culture_lookup[str(subj_i)]
    culture_j = culture_lookup[str(subj_j)]
    same_culture = (culture_i == culture_j)

    for e1 in labels:
        e1 = e1.lower()
        vec_i = processed_maps[subj_i][e1]    # flattened, contains NaNs

        for e2 in labels:
            e2 = e2.lower()
            vec_j = processed_maps[subj_j][e2]

            key = (subj_i, subj_j, e1, e2)

            if key in done_keys:
                continue

            valid = ~np.isnan(vec_i) & ~np.isnan(vec_j)

            rho, _ = spearmanr(vec_i[valid], vec_j[valid])

            pair_rows.append({
                "pair_subj": (subj_i, subj_j),
                "pair_emo": (e1, e2),
                "subj_i": subj_i,
                "subj_j": subj_j,
                "emotion1": e1,
                "emotion2": e2,
                "matched": (e1 == e2),
                "same_culture": same_culture,
                "rho": rho
            })

            done_keys.add(key)
            n_new += 1

    if n_pair % SAVE_INTERVAL == 0:
        print(f"[Autosave] Processed {n_pair}/{total_pairs} subject pairs "
              f"(+{n_new} new correlations).")

        pd.DataFrame(pair_rows).to_csv(output_path, index=False)
        print(f"Saved to {output_path}")

        n_new = 0

# FINAL SAVE
df_final = pd.DataFrame(pair_rows)
df_final.to_csv(output_path, index=False)

print("\n===============================================")
print(f"Final save complete.")
print(f"Total correlations: {len(df_final)}")
print(f"Saved to: {output_path}")
print("===============================================")

df_final.head()
```

Moreover, The distribution of correlation values in each condition was calculated. The result suggested a large variance of correlation values across all conditions, resembling normal distributions, with the sample mean being very close to zero.

```{python}
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

# Make sure rho is numeric
df_final["rho"] = pd.to_numeric(df_final["rho"], errors="coerce")

conditions = [
    (True,  True,  "matched = True,  same_culture = True"),
    (True,  False, "matched = True,  same_culture = False"),
    (False, True,  "matched = False, same_culture = True"),
    (False, False, "matched = False, same_culture = False"),
]

for matched_val, same_cult_val, title in conditions:
    subset = df_final[
        (df_final["matched"] == matched_val) &
        (df_final["same_culture"] == same_cult_val)
    ]["rho"].dropna()

    plt.figure()
    plt.hist(subset, bins=30)
    plt.title(title)
    plt.xlabel("Spearman r")
    plt.ylabel("Count")
    plt.tight_layout()

    plt.savefig('plot.png')

    plt.show()

   
```


## Discussion

### Summary of Replication Attempt

The confimatory analysis showed close-to-zero mean correlation values in both of the conditions (*r*=0.044 for different culture same emotion condition, and *r*=0.028 for different culture different emotion condition). The values themselves are very different from the correlations reported in the original study (*r*=0.7 for different culture same emotion condition, and *r*=0.4), nor the difference between the two conditions are significant enough to require a statistical test. Therefore, we failed to replicate the original result.

### Exploratory Analysis
We conducted to exploratory analysis. First, calculated mean correlation values for within culture condition to compare the correlation differences across between-and within-culture conditions. However, the two conditions also showed close-to-zero mean correlation values (*r*=0.042 for same culture same emotion condition, and *r*=0.027 for same culture different emotion condition). The differences between the two conditions are also not significant enough to require a statistical test. 

Second, we also examined the distribution of correlation values across four conditions. All of the correlation showed wide range of variations with normal-like distribution and most of the values being close to zero. 

### Commentary

These results, altogether, could suggest more emotionwise/participantwise variations in this data sample to the original sample. Indeed, the visualization of BSMs suggest some possible cross-cultural differences for emotions like disgust, sadness, and surprise. Another possibility is that this replication attempt might have ommitted some procedures in processing the data for the main analyses, as the methods for the particular experiment we attempted to replicate (experiment 1c) was described vaguely and quite short in the original paper.
